query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Elevated temperature oxidation of a non‐equilibrium Mg–containing HEA drives selective surface segregation where Ti, due to its higher oxygen affinity, forms a continuous TiO₂-rich passivating oxide layer that counteracts the deleterious effects of Mg oxidation, thereby reducing corrosion rates and modifying high‐temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast, metastable Mg–containing HEA with a homogeneous distribution of constituent elements including Ti, Mg, Al, and Zn.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidation treatment at 600 °C for 1 hour in an oxygen‐controlled environment (oxygen partial pressure ≈0.1 atm).
generation.conditions: High‐temperature oxidation under constant oxygen partial pressure; comparisons are made between the pre-oxidized homogeneous state and the post-oxidation surface–segregated state.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation of Ti resulting in the formation of a continuous, adherent, and TiO₂-rich oxide layer, while Mg remains predominantly in the bulk or forms discontinuous oxides.
generation.mechanism: At 600 °C, differences in oxygen affinity and diffusion kinetics cause Ti to preferentially migrate toward the surface and oxidize to form a dense, protective TiO₂ layer. This TiO₂ passivation reduces active sites for corrosion despite the presence of Mg, whose oxidation typically produces a less protective scale. The resulting oxide morphology thereby enhances overall corrosion resistance and modifies subsequent oxidation behavior at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, oxidized samples will exhibit roughly a 30% reduction in corrosion current density and display a more uniform, continuous oxide scale enriched in TiO₂, as evidenced by surface elemental mapping and phase analysis.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast alloy with a homogeneous elemental distribution prior to oxidation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies under oxidation conditions at temperatures around 600 °C and at an oxygen partial pressure near 0.1 atm; significantly higher temperatures or oxygen pressures might induce alternative phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: Although selective Ti segregation is supported by trends in similar multicomponent systems, the precise quantitative improvement (approx. 30% reduction) may vary with small compositional differences. The primary focus on Ti is justified as its oxygen affinity dominates over Mg under these conditions, even though Mg also influences the overall oxidation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Oxidize identical samples at 600 °C for 1 hour under 0.1 atm O₂ and subsequently compare the surface composition (using XPS and atom probe tomography) and corrosion behavior (via electrochemical polarization tests) of oxidized versus unoxidized samples.
measurements: Surface elemental mapping and phase identification (XPS/APT)
Corrosion potential and current density via electrochemical polarization
Measurement of oxide scale thickness and uniformity using TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized samples do not demonstrate a significant (≥25–30%) Ti enrichment at the surface or a corresponding reduction in corrosion metrics relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 2 shows a CoCrFeNiMn alloy constituting a single-phase FCC structure that is oxidized at 400 °C for 120 min. A relatively lower temperature compared to past studies is chosen for this study to suppress the phase transformation tendency in this super-saturated alloy. The thin oxide film (~20 nm) forms a compositionally layered structure. Starting from the equiatomic base alloy, a Ni-enriched layer is followed by Cr-rich oxide followed by Fe, Mn, and Co-rich oxide layers (Fig. 1g). The enrichment of elements in the top layer, however, is not uniform. While the Mn layer appears on the top, at certain locations, bubble-like Fe pockets can be seen on the top layer of the surface (Fig. 2b). Furthermore, due to the solid-state nature of the oxidation, atomic diffusion from the bulk alloy results in the formation of defects within inner layers (Fig. 2c). Unlike liquids, solid surfaces undergo elastic deformation as atoms diffuse through to form the oxide layer. This study investigated the effects of composition and processing on the microstructure, hardness, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of spark plasma sintered Mg-Ti-Zn alloys. Key findings include: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn alloys were produced via ball milling and spark plasma sintering. XRD, SEM, and STEM analyses revealed the presence of multiple phases. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high hardness and stiffness, which were much higher than those of any commercial Mg alloy. Both TZ and 4TZ exhibited high corrosion resistance (indicated by the high corrosion potential and low corrosion current density) and passivation, which were attributed to the formation of a Ti rich surface film. These findings demonstrate the potential of combining mechanical alloying and SPS to engineer Mg-containing multi-principal element alloys with a rare combination of high hardness and corrosion resistance. This strategy offers a new pathway for designing lightweight structural or biomedical materials that overcome the traditional strength–corrosion trade-off in Mg and Zn alloys. papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.approach: Combined CALPHAD analysis, non‐equilibrium solidification and kinetic (diffusion‐driven precipitation) simulations along with induction furnace casting and heat treatments; extensive microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM)
papers.findings: Both alloys exhibited multiphase microstructures comprising primary solid solutions with significant portions of intermetallic compounds (e.g. Mg2Si, Al9Mn2Si). The work identified sequential invariant transformations and indicated that different processing routes promote distinct phase evolution sequences.
papers.mechanism: Non-equilibrium processing leads to diffusion-driven precipitation and sequential stabilization of intermetallic phases from the supersaturated solid solution, with processing conditions governing the order of phase formation.

papers.title: Microstructure, Phase Formation and Heat-Treating of Novel Cast Al-Mg-Zn-Cu-Si Lightweight Complex Concentrated Aluminum Based Alloy.
papers.approach: Utilized CALPHAD-based design, gravity permanent mold casting and controlled heat treatments; characterization via SEM, XRD and mechanical testing
papers.findings: The alloy exhibits a multiphase microstructure with a primary α-Al solid solution reinforced by intermetallic phases (e.g. Mg2Si, Al2Cu). Heat treatments induced transformations that correlated with changes in hardness, compression strength and electrical conductivity.
papers.mechanism: Thermal processing drives the evolution from a metastable non-equilibrium state toward a stabilized distribution of intermetallic compounds, influencing not only mechanical properties but also potentially the corrosion and oxidation behaviors through altered phase distributions.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: MgTiZn and Mg4TiZn multi‐principal element alloys
papers.approach: Employed high-energy ball milling coupled with spark plasma sintering (SPS) to synthesize alloys; microstructure characterization by XRD, SEM, STEM; electrochemical corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization, immersion)
papers.findings: Both alloy variants exhibited high hardness and stiffness, with refined multiphase microstructures. Notably, a Ti-rich surface film (likely TiO2) was observed, which correlated with high corrosion resistance, as indicated by favorable corrosion potentials and low corrosion current densities.
papers.mechanism: Intensive mechanical alloying and rapid consolidation induce a non-equilibrium microstructure that evolves to promote surface segregation. This segregation facilitates the formation of a protective, passivating Ti-rich oxide film, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.

papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Quinary lightweight HEAs containing Al, Be, Mg, Ti with variations (Cu, Si, Li)
papers.approach: High-throughput DFT calculations combined with Grand Canonical Linear Programming (GCLP) to evaluate formation energies and phase stability at 0 K and room temperature
papers.findings: Identified promising compositions that exhibit a single solid solution phase with low densities and high specific stiffness. However, several compositions are metastable at room temperature, implying that rapid processing (e.g. fast cooling) is required to preserve the non-equilibrium state.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamic and electronic factors, including configurational entropy contributions, dictate whether a non-equilibrium solid solution can be stabilized or will decompose into intermetallic compounds; the presence of Mg plays a key role in these phase equilibria.

papers.title: Characterisation of a Novel Complex Concentrated Alloy for Marine Applications.
papers.approach: Designed via simulation (CALPHAD) and produced by induction furnace and pour mold casting; subsequent heat treatment and comprehensive microstructural, mechanical and corrosion characterization
papers.findings: The alloy shows a dendritic α-Al matrix with interdendritic intermetallic phases (notably Al2Cu and Zn-based solid solutions). It offers significantly enhanced mechanical properties and exhibits corrosion rates several times lower than conventional steels, attributed to optimal phase distribution.
papers.mechanism: Controlled phase evolution via thermal processing leads to a refined and uniformly distributed intermetallic network that enhances passivation, thereby influencing both corrosion resistance and the behavior under high-temperature oxidation.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high entropy alloy (model system for complex alloys)
papers.approach: Conducted controlled oxidation experiments at 400 °C under low oxygen pressures; employed in situ atom probe tomography (APT), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) analyses
papers.findings: Observed the rapid formation of a thin (~20 nm) layered oxide film with compositional gradients (initial Ni-rich layer followed by Cr-rich and then Fe/Co/Mn-rich oxide layers). The study detailed how atomic diffusion and redox potential differences drive the evolution of the oxide scale.
papers.mechanism: The oxidation process initiates from selective elemental segregation based on atomic sizes and redox potentials. Over time, diffusional kinetics result in layered oxide structures that govern the protective nature of the scale, providing insights potentially applicable to Mg-containing systems.

established: Lightweight high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with densities below 6 g/cm3 can be achieved by incorporating Mg along with other low-density elements.
Non-equilibrium processing (e.g., rapid solidification, mechanical alloying) commonly results in multiphase microstructures that include both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds.
Computational tools like CALPHAD, DFT, and first-principles-based methods can effectively predict phase stability and transformation pathways in these complex alloys.

Tailored microstructural evolution (via controlled heat treatments or processing routes) can enhance mechanical properties and corrosion resistance by influencing the formation and distribution of passive oxide films.

approaches_tried.approach: Induction furnace casting with subsequent heat treatment guided by CALPHAD and kinetic simulations
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful formation of multiphase alloys with predictable solid solution and intermetallic distributions; offers insight into diffusion-driven precipitation kinetics.

approaches_tried.approach: High-energy ball milling combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS)
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced refined Mg-containing alloys with high corrosion resistance due to passivating Ti-rich surface films, albeit with complex phase segregations.

approaches_tried.approach: First-principles DFT coupled with high-throughput screening (GCLP)
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified promising metastable single-phase compositions and quantified the role of configurational entropy in phase stabilization.

mechanisms: Diffusion-driven precipitation leading to transformation from a metastable solid solution to a more stable distribution of intermetallic phases.
Surface segregation during non-equilibrium processing that promotes the formation of passivating oxide films (e.g., TiO2, Al2O3) which enhance corrosion resistance and affect oxidation behavior.
Thermodynamic stabilization via configurational entropy that can maintain metastable non-equilibrium phases under rapid cooling conditions.
Competition between species based on atomic size and redox potential dictating layered oxide scale formation during high-temperature oxidation.
disagreements: There is some divergence regarding the role of intermetallic compounds: while some studies suggest that a uniform, refined intermetallic distribution enhances corrosion resistance, others question whether such phases might accelerate localized corrosion through micro-galvanic effects.
Minor inconsistencies between CALPHAD/simulation predictions and experimental phase compositions indicate uncertainties in modeling diffusion and multi-element interactions in these complex systems.
The precise influence of specific alloying additions (e.g., the role of Al in altering oxidation kinetics) remains debated across different studies.
open_questions: How do metastable non-equilibrium states in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs evolve over time, particularly under varying thermal and environmental conditions?
What is the quantitative relationship between evolving intermetallic phase distributions and changes in corrosion as well as high-temperature oxidation behavior?
To what extent do processing parameters (e.g., cooling rate, heat-treatment conditions) dictate the eventual protective oxide film characteristics on these alloys?
How can computational predictions be refined to more accurately capture the kinetics of multi-phase evolution in these multicomponent systems?
opportunities: Combine rapid solidification methods with tailored heat treatments to 'freeze' desirable metastable states that favor beneficial phase distributions for corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Employ in situ characterization techniques (e.g., time-resolved TEM or APT during oxidation) to directly track phase evolution and oxide scale formation in Mg-containing HEAs.
Integrate computational (DFT, CALPHAD) and experimental approaches to optimize alloy compositions and processing routes for maximal corrosion resistance and high-temperature stability.

Explore synergistic effects of mechanical alloying followed by controlled thermal processing to manipulate surface segregation phenomena, thereby enabling predictive control over passivation layer development.

directions.direction: Diffusion‐driven precipitation of Mg‐rich intermetallics during post‐processing
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the evolution of a non‐equilibrium supersaturated state into a more stable multiphase one. Evidence from studies using CALPHAD and kinetic simulations (e.g. PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions) support the role of diffusion‐driven precipitation. It is well grounded in known diffusion kinetics and microgalvanic mechanisms affecting corrosion and oxidation.

directions.direction: Surface segregation driving formation of a passivating oxide layer
directions.assessment: This direction focuses on how selective elemental diffusion (for instance, Ti enrichment) during high‐temperature oxidation creates a continuous, protective oxide film. Prior observations (e.g. PMC12299034::web::035::4_conclusions and PMC11169556::web::008::results_and_discussion) support that segregation phenomena can alter surface oxide composition and thereby corrosion/oxidation behavior. It tightly couples thermodynamics, diffusion, and passivation kinetics.

directions.direction: Stress‐assisted phase separation invoking micro‐galvanic effects
directions.type: Mechanical Processing Coupled with Microstructure Evolution
directions.assessment: Introducing controlled deformation may accelerate phase separation. The resulting coarse intermetallics can serve as cathodic sites relative to the anodic matrix. This micro‐galvanic coupling is known to influence localized corrosion and oxidation (see PMC7579168::web::033::4_discussion and PMC12299034::web::035::4_conclusions). Although the mechanism is slightly more complex, it offers a direct route to link mechanical processing, microstructure and functional performance.

directions.direction: Time‐dependent natural aging transformation from a supersaturated state to equilibrium intermetallic distribution
directions.assessment: This proposal examines how the as-cast, non-equilibrium state evolves over months at room temperature. Evidence from kinetic simulations and CALPHAD studies (e.g. PMC10728166::web::052::energetical_stability) indicate that even ambient aging modifies phase fractions. This gradual evolution is expected to affect surface electrochemistry and passive film formation under corrosive and high‐temperature oxidation conditions.
